title: A shared timeout/deadline primitive, with hard-kill left to each capability
summary: A small library of pure functions owns timeout timing and classification (clamp a requested timeout, create a deadline, tell a timeout from a cancellation); each capability keeps its own hard kill. There is deliberately no central timeout service.
firstReason: Go's standard context package already provides deadlines, cancellation and a recorded cause, so a separate timeout library is unnecessary; the rule that each capability owns its own hard kill is kept.

title: One harness home resolver
summary: One resolver decides where harness user data lives: an explicitly configured path, then the DSH_HOME variable, then ~/.dsh. An empty variable counts as unset, and all user data stays under that one root.
firstReason: A single home resolver prevents components from disagreeing about where data lives, and it is trivial to keep in Go.

title: One outbound proxy policy, installed before anything can request
summary: One outbound proxy policy is resolved once from the launch environment and installed globally before any plugin can make a request, because Node's fetch ignores the proxy variables. The project's .env file may not set a proxy.
firstReason: Go's HTTP client honours the proxy variables by default, so nothing has to be installed globally; the Go design keeps the policy (resolved once from the launch snapshot, project .env refused) by giving every component one shared HTTP transport.

title: Public package manifest fields
summary: One public type describes the package.json fields the harness reads for a plugin (name, version, engines and the dsh section); internal packaging metadata is deliberately left out of it.
firstReason: Plugin authors still need one documented manifest, but an external plugin is a process with its own manifest file, not an npm package, so the format is new.

title: Ship experimental capabilities as optional bundles
summary: Experimental and optional capabilities are offered as default-off 'optional bundles' on the plugins page, each with an icon and a localized title. Their dependencies ship with every installation, so a bundle is admitted only if it adds no heavy runtime and works without extra configuration.
firstReason: The goal stands: experimental capabilities are visible and one switch away, not hand-installed. In Go every first-party capability is already compiled in, so an optional bundle is a named, default-off configuration group; the admission test becomes binary size and external executables, not npm download cost.

title: Incremental tool-argument scanning and argument order during preparation
summary: While a tool call's arguments are still streaming, a lazy scanner indexes top-level keys and reads only the fields the display asks for, without parsing the whole JSON. Tool schemas put short descriptive fields before long ones so that they arrive first.
firstReason: The preparing stage needs a path or a description before the full argument exists, and re-parsing a growing JSON text on every delta costs quadratic time. In Go the scanner runs in the host that renders the row; the argument-order rule is about model behaviour and carries as is.

title: Shared time vocabulary for wall-clock selectors
summary: One utility package owns the time vocabulary accepted at boundaries: strict instant and zone parsers, durations, and bounded cron and recurrence-rule (RRULE) values. Parsers return 'accepted' or 'rejected' with a stable reason code, and each caller maps the reason to its own error text.
firstReason: Three packages had grown private, slightly different parsers. One Go package with typed reasons gives the same result; part of it is covered by the standard `time` package, the recurrence rules are not.

title: Discover Official bundles without installing their runtimes
summary: The Claude Code and Codex subagent integrations appear in an installation-owned catalog with embedded metadata and icons, so they can be discovered offline, but their runtimes are installed only when the user selects them.
firstReason: The goal stands: heavy integrations are discoverable but not paid for by everyone. Inference: in Go the integration code is small and compiled in; what is 'on demand' is the external agent program it drives, so the catalog entry reports whether that executable is present instead of installing an npm package.

title: Keep the HarnessError base in a dependency-free package
summary: The `HarnessError` base class lives in a package with no dependencies, because the tool registry records an error's name and code only when the thrown value is an instance of that one class. `dsh-llm` re-exports it so both import paths name one constructor.
firstReason: The goal (every expected failure carries a stable code the tool registry can record, without pulling in the LLM runtime) stands. Go has no class-identity problem: a small error interface in a leaf package, checked with `errors.As`, gives the same result and needs no re-export.

title: Plugin market index format
summary: A market is one JSON index document, kept separate from whatever generates it. The format reuses npm package names, versions, ranges, distribution tags and person declarations, and adds localized titles, categories and labels.
firstReason: One self-contained index document that third parties can publish is a good shape. Its identity fields are npm's; Go plugins are processes or MCP servers (DH-ADR-4) and the Go design need not keep the file format (DH-ADR-2), so the index needs identity and version fields of its own.

title: Plugin detail documents
summary: A plugin's long description is read in a fixed order: the Markdown file named by `meta.detail` in the package's locale file for the display language, then shorter language prefixes, then English, then the package README, and for a market entry the README of its repository directory.
firstReason: A detail page with a deterministic, localized fallback order is worth keeping. The lookup is defined over npm package layout and locale JSON files; under DH-ADR-4 a plugin is a process package with its own manifest, so the order is stated again over that manifest.

title: Harness home path categories
summary: Proposal, not finished upstream: group every path under the harness home directory into `config`, `data`, `state`, `cache` and `backup` categories modelled on the XDG Base Directory Specification, all still inside the home, with one path helper that every package uses. Well-known top-level entries such as `.env` and `sessions/` keep their places.
firstReason: Adopt. The Go design lays out its home directory from scratch (DH-ADR-2), so it can start with categories and one resolver at no migration cost; the categories tell an operator what is safe to delete and what must be backed up.

title: Ship optional bundles with the installation
summary: The installation ships a named list of optional bundles (official but experimental layers such as Agent Teams) that are switched off until the user turns them on in the plugin page; they can never be removed, and they are the one declared exception to the rule that the default product contains nothing experimental.
firstReason: The goal stands: a user can switch on an official optional capability without finding and installing it by name. With compiled-in components (DH-ADR-4) the capability is already in the binary, so "shipped but off" becomes a component that the default configuration leaves disabled and the plugin page can enable; the npm runtime-dependency mechanics do not carry over.
